items.title: Momentum versus kinetic energy
items.draft: A car travels around a circular track at constant speed. (a) Does its kinetic energy change? (b) Does its momentum change? (c) If the car doubles its speed, by what factors do its momentum magnitude and kinetic energy change? Explain.
items.internal_rationale: Constant KE, changing momentum direction; doubling speed doubles momentum magnitude and quadruples KE.

items.title: Stopping versus rebounding
items.draft: A 0.20-kg ball approaches a wall at 5.0 m/s. In one collision it stops; in another it rebounds at 5.0 m/s along the same line. (a) Find the magnitude and direction of the ball’s momentum change in each case. (b) If the collisions last equally long, which produces the greater average net force on the ball, and by what factor?
items.internal_rationale: Momentum changes 1.0 and 2.0 kg m/s away from wall; rebound gives twice average net force.

items.title: Same force: equal time versus equal distance
items.draft: Two carts of different masses start at rest on a level, frictionless track. Each is pushed with the same constant horizontal force. (a) If the forces act for the same time, do the carts gain the same momentum or the same kinetic energy? (b) If the forces instead act through the same distance, do the carts gain the same momentum or the same kinetic energy? Explain.
items.internal_rationale: Same time gives equal momentum gains, unequal KE. Same distance gives equal KE gains, unequal momenta. Distinct from simple force-duration tradeoff already retained.

items.title: Propulsion without air
items.draft: An astronaut is at rest relative to a nearby spacecraft and is holding a tool. (a) Can the astronaut start moving toward the spacecraft merely by moving their arms and legs, without releasing anything? (b) In which direction should the astronaut throw the tool to move toward the spacecraft? Explain using conservation of momentum, neglecting external forces during these actions.
items.internal_rationale: Internal motions do not change astronaut+tool COM momentum; throw tool away from spacecraft. Clarify wording in drafting if needed: moving limbs can move other body parts, but cannot produce sustained translation of the whole system.

items.title: Distinguish elastic outcomes
items.draft: A cart moving at 4.0 m/s strikes an identical cart initially at rest on a level, frictionless track. Consider two proposed outcomes: A, the first cart stops and the second moves at 4.0 m/s; B, both carts move at 2.0 m/s in the original direction. (a) Which outcomes conserve momentum? (b) Which conserve kinetic energy? (c) Which could describe an elastic collision? Explain.
items.internal_rationale: Both conserve momentum; only A conserves KE. Simple checks, no simultaneous quadratic solution.

items.title: Simple perfectly inelastic collision
items.draft: A 0.50-kg cart moving at 4.0 m/s collides with an identical cart initially at rest on a level, frictionless track. They stick together. (a) Find their common final velocity. (b) Calculate the total kinetic energy before and after the collision. (c) Where can the missing kinetic energy go? (d) Why can the carts not both come to rest?
items.internal_rationale: Final 2.0 m/s original direction; KE 4.0 J to 2.0 J; internal energy/sound/deformation; zero final momentum would violate initial nonzero momentum. Can refer to preceding elastic question rather than repeat setup at implementation.
